summary: Discovery call to understand Silverlode's network posture and constraints for a Private/VPC deployment of Redwood inference. Key topics: transit peering, private endpoints, egress NAT, region gating for data residency, and fallback to dedicated hosted nodes. Customer has strict egress IP whitelisting and multi-region data residency requirement; wants a plan that supports a UK primary region and failover to Ireland with no cross-border data leakage.
topics: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway bridging
Egress IPs, NAT gateways, and firewall rules
SLA and canary fallback to Dedicated capacity
transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-04-11 16:00 UTC, duration 62m. Attendees: James Park (Redwood AE), Elena Torres (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CSM); Rajiv Menon (Silverlode VP Eng), Sara Li (Cloud Architect), Tom Hsu (Security).

[00:00] James Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining. quick round of intros, then we'll go into the network constraints and the region gating you sent over, thanks for that.
[00:23] Rajiv Menon: Yeah thanks James. we're on a tight timeline, aiming to have a pilot in the UK region by end of quarter. we can't allow tokens or logs to leave UK data centers. so region gating is big.
[00:40] Sara Li: Also on our side we have static egress IPs required for our customers' firewalls. we use a transit gateway + NAT pairs across two AZs, so any private service needs to come from those IPs.
[01:05] Elena Torres: Got it. For Redwood Private we support private endpoints and VPC peering. There are two common patterns: one is direct VPC peering from your VPC to our managed VPC per region; the other is transit gateway attachment. Peering is simpler but you hit route limits at scale.
[01:30] Tom Hsu: Are there any protocol restrictions? our security team dislikes overly permissive SGs.
[01:40] Elena Torres: We recommend least-privilege: only allow outbound HTTPS to our private endpoint IPs and VPC endpoint routes. We'll produce a minimal SG example.
[01:55] Rajiv Menon: Can you explain how failover looks? If the UK region has an outage we need failover to Ireland but we also can't copy logs across borders.
[02:10] James Park: Sure. There are two approaches. one is active-active with routing controls that ensure data residency — harder. more common is active-passive: primary in UK, standby in IE. We can route traffic via your control plane or have an on-prem routing policy to switch endpoints. Redwood's private control plane can be run in-region for compliance, or we can provide a control-plane proxy.
[02:40] Sara Li: If we use active-passive, what happens to KV cache and model state? do we have to warm caches in Ireland explicitly?
[02:52] Elena Torres: Yes, KV cache isn't automatically replicated cross-region. You'll either accept cold-starts or run a small warm pool in the standby region. For cost reasons some customers run tiny dedicated nodes in standby to keep model warm.
[03:10] Rajiv Menon: And latency sensitivity — our SLAs target 150ms p95 for short prompts. is that realistic in a VPC peering setup?
[03:25] Elena Torres: In-region peering typically meets that. The main variables are instance type, quantization profile, and batching. We can share our benchmark matrix.
[03:40] Tom Hsu: On authentication — we need SAML SSO and role-based access and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[03:50] Maya Chen: Redwood supports SAML/SSO for Console and mTLS for service-to-service. Audit logs can be pushed to your logging endpoint or delivered via S3 with KMS encryption. We also support forwarding syslog to a customer collector.
[04:10] Rajiv Menon: KMS — will Redwood use our KMS keys or your managed keys for model artifacts and logs?
[04:20] James Park: For Private deployments you can bring your KMS/HSM. We support wrapping of secrets with your KMS. We'll put this in the security pack.
[04:30] Sara Li: Ok good. now networking specifics: we have a NAT pool 203.0.113.40/29 that needs to be the egress addresses for any outbound calls. can we ensure Redwood's nodes originate from those IPs?
[04:48] Elena Torres: If you peer to our VPC we will see routes back but the egress IPs will be our managed egress unless you force egress through your NAT by using proxying. The pattern we recommend is to run Redwood Private inside your VPC or in a VPC you control via an appliance/helm chart — then egress naturally comes from your NAT.
[05:12] Rajiv Menon: Wait, em, so are you saying our preferred model is either full private deployment in our VPC or a managed VPC with private endpoints where egress is still Redwood's?
[05:25] Elena Torres: Exactly. There is also a hybrid where the control plane is hosted but data plane runs in your VPC — that's the middle ground: you retain egress and KMS while Redwood handles orchestration.
[05:40] Tom Hsu: That hybrid sounds promising. will that need peering or a private endpoint?
[05:48] Elena Torres: Typically that uses interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for the control plane, and the data plane nodes are in customer subnets. We'll provide terraform modules to automate.
[06:05] Sara Li: One more question on route limits and overlapping CIDRs. our VPC uses 10.0.0.0/16; our corp VPC uses 10.1.0.0/16. what if your managed VPC uses 10.0.0.0/8?
[06:20] Elena Torres: We avoid overlapping by assigning unique CIDRs per private deployment. If you're using our managed VPC we can negotiate non-overlap, but many customers prefer bringing their own VPC to avoid this.
[06:35] Rajiv Menon: Any constraints for multi-region peering? like transit gateway attachment costs?
[06:45] James Park: Transit Gateway is supported; it's often used by large enterprises. note there are extra egress charges and cross-AZ bandwidth implications. We can estimate cost based on expected TPS and egress GB.
[07:02] Sara Li: Does Redwood support static BGP for on-prem connectivity? we're thinking of a colo hop for low latency to partner networks.
[07:13] Elena Torres: We don't provide BGP termination in the hosted model, but in Private/on-prem deployments we can accept BGP sessions via the customer's edge device if required. We'll need the network team to do a handoff for that.
[07:30] Rajiv Menon: Security review — SOC2 evidence, pen test reports, and a data flow diagram. can we get those?
[07:38] Maya Chen: Yes we'll attach SOC2 type II, recent pentest summary, and a redacted dataflow for Private. Also a KMS integration guide.
[07:50] Tom Hsu: How do rollouts and canary deployments work in Private? can we do blue/green with automatic fallback to a hosted model if private capacity fails?
[08:05] James Park: We support canary and A/B style rollouts via our Console. For Private you can define fallback policies — if capacity is exceeded we can route to a compatible model variant in Redwood Hosted or Dedicated. We'll show the routing policy examples.
[08:25] Sara Li: Is there any risk of PII being sent to hosted fallback? that's a compliance no-no.
[08:32] Elena Torres: Then you should configure strict routing to avoid fallback to hosted. Alternatively, we can map your tenant to dedicated capacity (reserved) so fallbacks remain within your Dedicated pool.
[08:47] Rajiv Menon: Let's talk about perf testing. can we run a lab to validate p95 and token throughput from our VPC across peering and transit?
[08:58] James Park: Absolutely. We'll schedule a benchmark with three scenarios: direct peering in-region, transit gateway in-region, and cross-region (UK->IE) failover. We'll need your test harness and some sample prompts.
[09:16] Tom Hsu: For the benchmarks we'll need packet captures and latency breakdowns. can you expose per-token latencies in traces?
[09:24] Elena Torres: Yes our Console has trace hooks and per-token breakdowns; we can export traces and flamegraphs, though raw pcap we'd coordinate offline for security reasons.
[09:36] Rajiv Menon: Ok that helps. About cost: do you have guidance for the warm-pool standby nodes cost vs accepting cold starts?
[09:46] James Park: We'll produce a cost model: standby minimal nodes for warm cache vs on-demand cold start latencies. generally if you need sub-200ms p95 you want warm standby for frequent traffic.
[09:58] Sara Li: Any requirement on subnets and ENIs? our subnets are /24 only; will that suffice?
[10:07] Elena Torres: Usually yes, but if you plan lots of pods or instances we recommend /22. We'll add subnet sizing guidance in the network checklist.
[10:20] Rajiv Menon: A couple of odd constraints: some of our customers require that logs be forwarded to a SIEM in-country only, not to S3 in another region. can Redwood support region-restricted log delivery?
[10:33] Maya Chen: Yes, for Private deployments logs can be stored in customer-owned buckets in-country, or forwarded to your SIEM endpoint. We'll document delivery patterns.
[10:45] James Park: Quick recap — items we will send: region availability matrix, network checklist, terraform module examples, SOC2 + pentest, and a proposal for a benchmark. Anything to add?
[10:58] Sara Li: please include egress IP mapping options and a recommended pattern for our transit gateway setup.
[11:06] Rajiv Menon: and an explicit data-residency readme for the active-passive failover scenario.
[11:12] James Park: noted.
[11:20] Tom Hsu: One last thing — are there any known incompatibilities with our vendor firewall (AegisWall)? we've had trouble with healthchecks through PrivateLink before.
[11:32] Elena Torres: We've seen vendor-specific quirks, usually around path MTU and TLS inspection. We'll add a vendor compatibility note and suggested firewall rules.
[11:44] Rajiv Menon: ok thanks everyone. next steps: we'll gather CIDRs and NAT IPs and set up the benchmark slot.
[11:54] James Park: Great; we'll follow up with the docs and propose times for the benchmark.

Auto-generated action items (end): James to send region matrix; Elena to prepare terraform runbook; Sara to send CIDRs.

End of transcript.
